PART 2: Yall had questions, so here’s my answers!
1. Soil health and seed quality MATTER!✨
When I use an organic seed STARTING mix and quality seed, like @johnnys_seeds, I have the most success with starting any seed. It’s worth every penny. (Especially considering my time)

2. Cold environment ✨
I did two successions (by accident) and combined they gave me 47/50 seeds with germination! Again, thank you @johnnys_seeds Both ways I had sprinkled the seeds on top of MOIST soil and lightly covered-per the seed package. The first was in a dark cold room that acts like a cellar—it’s attached to my house but it’s not heated. The temperatures fluctuate with the outside, but it never freezes. Half of them sprouted this way. The other half, I set my container that had my seeds/soil in it and placed it on top of my deep freezer with indirect grow light. I got the other half germinated! 

3. Room to grow ✨
Once they sprouted, I plucked them out of the container and into their own DEEP cells. I did a split between 2” plastic cells and large soil block—both did great. 

4. Soil Health MATTERS ✨
Seed starting mix, growing soil, and outdoor soil! I use organic seed starting soil, Promix series when I pot up, and my hubby buried compost 4-6” deep where I planted the transplants! 

5. Stake & net!!! ✨ 
If you want tall straight stems—you have to do this. 

6. Timeline ✨
I started them late January, under grow lights in February, hardened off and transplanted mid April (last expected frost), and they started to bloom end of June and are still going into middle of July! 

I’m zone 7

Celosia might be one of the most underrated flowers I grow.

It loves the sun, handles heat and dry spells once established, comes in the most incredible colors and textures, and just keeps going when so many other flowers start looking tired.

But what really earns it a spot in my garden? I can cut it for bouquets, dry it for arrangements, and mine reseeds so I often get volunteers the following year.

And that velvety texture? Nothing else in the garden looks quite like it.

If you’re planning next year’s flower garden, put celosia on your list. You won’t regret it. 🌸

Growing strawflowers has become one of my greatest joys every summer, so much so that I gave up a row of dahlia growing space (gasp! 😂) to make room for a strawflower rainbow this season. I love to use fresh strawflowers in arrangements, but what I love even more is having dried strawflowers on hand for holiday tablescapes and to fill antique jars and bowls to the brim with color year-round. I find their crunchy texture so satisfying.

My hopes and dreams for what I’ll do with this year’s strawflower crop: wreaths, garland, ornaments.
Realistically what I’ll do with this year’s strawflower crop: next to nothing (except admire them, of course, which is more than enough).

Meet ‘Linen’—a dreamy new zinnia variety developed by the breeding team at Johnny’s Selected Seeds, grown from seed right here at The Petal Patch. 🤍🌱

These blooms feel like summer dressed in her softest neutrals. Each flower opens into layer upon layer of full, dahlia-shaped petals in the most delicate blend of warm oatmeal, buttery cream, antique blush, pale peach, and the faintest touch of dusty pink along the edges. No two stems are exactly alike—some lean golden and sun-washed, while others deepen into rosy, vintage tones as they mature.

The texture is just as beautiful as the color: ruffled, densely petaled, and wonderfully imperfect, with every bloom carrying its own little personality. Together, they look like a bundle of faded silk, old ribbon, and warm linen caught in the afternoon light.

Flower feature: meet Ballerina! 🤍 A new zinnia variety we’ve been trying out this year!

Ballerina has become the star of so many bouquets and has been dancing circles in hearts. We are loving their fluffy petals that come in a variety of blush pink and peachy colors, plus their perfect size and wow-factor.

Safe to say, Ballerina has earned a future spot in our flower fields! 😍 do you agree?!

Your fall garden isn’t planted by counting backward from your first frost date alone. 

It’s also racing something called the Persephone Period. It’s the part of the year when daylight falls below 10 hours.

With so little light, most plants don’t necessarily die, but their growth slows dramatically. That means the spinach, carrots, kale, or lettuce you hope to harvest later needs to be nearly mature before those short days arrive.

And every crop needs a different head start.

That’s why the “days to maturity” printed on the seed packet can be misleading for fall planting. It reflects growing under better spring conditions, not increasingly shorter, cooler days.

Here’s the easier way to plan:

1. Find the last day your location receives 10 hours of daylight.
2. Choose what you want to grow.
3. Count backward using that crop’s recommended planting window.
4. Plant early enough for it to size up before growth slows.
